title: Modularize continuous batcher plugins and atomic KV rotation
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Motivation:
The current continuous-batcher implementation mixes policy, admission control, and KV lifecycle concerns in a single monolithic module. This makes iterative improvements slow, increases the risk of regressions during dependency upgrades (RocksDB/mmap/shim), and complicates per-tenant tuning. We also see periodic tail latency spikes tied to KV rotation/compaction where readers can observe transiently inconsistent slot indices during shard swaps. Finally, the scheduler’s coarse global lock for batch slot allocation contributes to contention at high QPS.

Goals:
1) Introduce a small, backward-compatible plugin interface for the continuous batcher so we can iterate batching/admission/prefetch strategies without touching core commitpath. 2) Implement an "atomic KV rotation" mechanism (epoched handle + swap-step) to ensure readers never see a partially-rotated shard and to decouple compaction from the primary read path. 3) Reduce scheduler contention by moving to per-worker allocation queues with cooperative yielding and fallbacks. 4) Perform targeted dependency upgrades required by the rotation code and mmap improvements with a clear rollback plan.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope includes API surface for plugin registration, a rotation coordinator component for KV shards, scheduler allocation rewrites, and upgrade testing for RocksDB and mmap-shim.
- Non-goal: complete rewrite of the batcher runtime (we aim for incremental, feature-flagged changes).

Deliverables:
- Batcher plugin interface + two implementations (legacy adapter + default policy).
- Rotation coordinator with atomic swap and background compaction worker.
- Per-worker scheduler queues and benchmarks.
- Upgrade path docs and a canary rollout plan.
acceptance_criteria: Plugin interface shims the current batcher and passes all existing unit/integration tests behind a feature flag
Atomic KV rotation prevents observed stale-read windows; measured false-positive stale-read rate reduced to 0 in unit tests and <1e-6 in load tests
95th percentile request tail under a sustained 3x baseline QPS improves by >=20% compared to baseline while CPU overhead does not exceed +5%
Scheduler contention metric (global-allocator-lock hold time) reduced by >=60% in perf harness
Dependency upgrades (RocksDB, mmap-shim, tokio) validated in CI matrix and documented rollback steps
Canary rollout executes without customer-facing errors; automatic rollback triggers validated

qa_steps: Run unit tests with feature flag off to verify backward compatibility: ./scripts/test --feature-flags off
Run integration suite with feature flag on against local RocksDB instance: ./scripts/integration --features atomic-rotation
Execute perf harness (k6) against canary cluster: ./infra/perf/run_k6.sh --scenario=kv-heavy --duration=30m
Simulate compaction and verify no stale reads by running the stale-read checker: ./tools/stale_read_check --workload=rotating-shard
Verify rollback: enable feature on canary, then disable and confirm state reconciles within 60s
notes: Implementation detail: rotation coordinator uses a two-phase swap: publish new shard reference under next-epoch, wait for inflight epoch drains, then atomically update the active-epoch pointer. This avoids pause-the-world semantics.
We will bump RocksDB in a dedicated change to avoid coupling; the rotation coordinator has an adapter layer so we can test old/new RocksDB side-by-side.

Scheduler change is intentionally minimal: per-worker queues plus a global slow-path that steals when local pools exhausted. This should preserve fairness while removing the hot global allocator lock.
Risk: private/on-prem customers running older kernels may not get mmap improvements; include a compatibility shim in the deployment bundle.
Rollback plan: feature flags and a migration toggle for epoch pointers. If issues detected, flip feature flag + force-drain workers; devs will run compaction rollback script located in attachments.
